heading: 12 The Bible and Japan
title_zh: 第十二章　聖經與日本
src: The new hall that the deshi had found housed Uchimura’s lecture meetings between 1919 and 1923. In it, Uchimura propounded his most famous biblical commentaries, and what would later come to be known as Mukyôkai slowly took shape. A description of the building itself and the nascent Mukyôkai introduces analysis of the lectures that kept its members coming.

The building, known as the Eiseikai Hall after its owners, the medical association, sat to the east of the Imperial Palace in Ôtemachi, across the street from the Home Ministry headquarters. After the Second World War, the telephone company took over the property. Uchimura described the Eiseikai Hall as a grand “German-style building,” second to none. A photograph introduces its three storeys, square except for rounded corners. It was built of stone facing, and a cupola topped the roof. Windows in the cupola admitted light and air into the hall below. Those entering ascended a “grand” circular staircase to the main floor. Eight men struggled to get a large piano up the stairs and into the hall. The piano was German and a source of great pride. Ochimura likened it to the lyre that Old Testament Psalmists used to praise the Lord. In this large hall, 700 people could worship with better light and ventilation than in the YMCA auditorium. Uchimura considered his four years there between the ages of fifty-nine and sixty-three the “high tide” of his career.

It was in these elegant surroundings that Uchimura’s group so proudly took the gospel downtown. There, between the huge new central railway station and the Imperial Palace, business leaders directed the national economy. For centuries, authorities had relegated Buddhist temples to the outer fringes of the city, so no one expected ecclesiastical organizations in a city centre. Mukyôkai’s resultant pride of place included a confidence that Christianity would flourish in Japan. The majesty of the hall required of both speakers and listeners great concentration. There Uchimura developed the mature style that made his lectures so memorable.

In the new hall, he could once again control who came to hear him. The masses who attended second coming lectures included those who simply walked in off the street. Advertising that brought them in appealed in part because it forecast imminent doom. After Uchimura had settled down to his new routine in the Eiseikai Hall, he needed some organization, if only to pay the high rent, to maximize the impact of the lectures, and to enable members to associate with each other. As the piano promoted pious praise rather than art, so both the surroundings and the lectures, Uchimura emphasized, should proclaim the greater glory of God.

The continuing popularity of Uchimura’s writings led many people to the new hall. By 1921, a membership system had been established. Since a clear identification with the group characterized Uchimura’s meetings from then on and continues to characterize the meetings of his followers, the nature of this first group merits attention.

Uchimura had strong convictions about who should attend. They should have read Seisho no Kenkyû for at least a year, pay a regular fee, realize that an absence of three months or more cancelled their membership, and dress appropriately for a serious lecture. No one should bother him during the two hours before a lecture. He required absolute silence. The lectures belong to all, he admonished, and to usurp the speaker’s attention for one’s personal business threatens the later total effect for the whole audience. To bring children under ten is “an unkindness to them, a distraction to the other listeners, and for the most part a great impediment to the speaker.” Attendance for the purpose of criticism or ridicule also harms the tenor of the meeting, so newspaper reporters are forbidden unless they come for their own edification. Finally, “come to pay consistent with your means. Truth that is not paid for will not endure. To hear a lecture free does not hurt the speaker but does hurt the listener. It is better not to hear a lecture for which you do not plan to pay.”

Although these prescriptions demanded much, they did not deter prospective members. On the Sunday when people could sign up for the first time, 560 responded, pledging to pay between ten sen and ten yen per month, with an average of l.2 yen. The monthly fee for those who paid at the top of the scale equalled about one-fourth of a workman’s salary. The deshi were willing and able to pay. The list of members that appeared the following month contained 650 names: 410 were men, of whom half were younger than twenty-five years, probably university students, along with several Buddhist priests. Membership peaked at 900. These statistics encouraged Uchimura because they reflected a continuing youthful interest in his lectures. Although the group may not have been the largest Japanese Christian audience, it was one of the largest, and its members possessed both sophistication and dedication.

For those who paid so dearly to attend, the surroundings and the lectures themselves had to provide a satisfactory religious experience. On one occasion, Uchimura gave Saitô an inventory of the care that ushers should exercise to seat people. They should sit correctly from the perspective of the speaker. Those “with an eager spirit and considerable age and length of affiliation [keireki] should occupy the first three rows.” Regular attendants should be discouraged from considering any seat “theirs,” for such an attitude lessens the “lively expectation [kakki kinshô]” of a service. In general, members should be seated from the front of the hall as they arrive. Many, particularly women, if left to their own devices, leave vacant the seats in the very front and the middle. Whether this results from egoism or false humility, it should be discouraged. In short, everything should help members of the audience to focus upon the message. Their concentration will in turn increase the speaker’s effectiveness.

To set the proper tone himself, Uchimura wore a black ensemble that included frock coat, vest, wing collar, four-in-hand tie, leather shoes, and homburg. Other speakers before him in each day’s program “provided variety.” They should not waste time. One of the youngest spent three minutes during a lecture flipping through his Bible to find a passage. Uchimura pointed out that a speaker who keeps 1,000 people waiting for three minutes wastes fifty hours in total. The speakers should also structure their talks carefully, putting the serious part of the lecture in the centre with a lighter introduction and conclusion. Uchimura also cautioned them to use the rhetorical devices of good speaking, including arm motions and humour, noting how Paul in Acts 20:35 displays his hands to demonstrate his economic independence. This concern for details combined care to do things the right way with controlled expression of emotion, both attributes highly valued by members of the audience.

Uchimura’s own lectures started with statements that all would support. Once nodding heads reflected common agreement, Uchimura would suddenly reverse himself and point out the weakness of accepted views before he started his alternative explanation. Recollections of those who heard the lectures indicate that his techniques succeeded. Shiga Naoya is quoted as saying that they wakened those who had drowsed off.

The intense attention to his words stimulated and fatigued Uchimura. “You hang on my words on Sunday mornings,” he said. “As a result, I want to give you everything I can. I had been feeling very tired on Mondays and could not understand why. Finally, the answer came: I wanted to give myself to those of you who listen so carefully. An inattentive audience doesn’t tire me.”

The congregation became tightly organized. Members had to give much and in return gained a strong sense of identity. The group resembled a Protestant church in many ways. The similarity increased when morning sessions replaced afternoon ones. Before the change in time, members could attend church in the morning and hear Uchimura in the afternoon. Now they had to choose. He had in practice given up the idea of reconciliation with established churches.

The lectures on the Bible delivered in the Eiseikai Hall became the high point of Uchimura’s career. Uchimura had conceived of Bible study as a vocation while a student in the United States and started it with his comments on Ruth in his first six months as a writer. During the succeeding thirty-seven years, he analyzed almost all sixty-six books of the Bible. The exceptions were all in the Old Testament: Nehemiah, Song of Solomon, Lamentations, and five of the minor prophets, Joel, Micah, Nahum, Haggai, and Malachi. Uchimura’s studies of the Bible still form the largest single corpus of commentaries on the Bible in the Japanese language. They include extensive analyses of Genesis, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, the four Gospels, and Romans. The studies of Job, Romans, and the four Gospels were originally prepared as lectures in the Eiseikai Hall.

A short series of lectures on Daniel in 1920 preceded these longer series. It gave Uchimura the chance to experiment with the format. He says that the view of history expressed in Daniel is important in understanding the New Testament attitude toward the end of the world. Yamamoto Taijirô recalls that Uchimura also considered it important because it told the members of the Christian community the sufferings that Christians can expect. After he finished with Daniel, Uchimura went quickly on to Job and Romans. They formed the core of his lectures in 1920 and 1922. The Life of Christ was completed over the four-year period 1922-25. These three sets of lectures taken together demonstrate his mature method. Selections from each of them follow. A fourth excerpt from the later commentary on Hosea demonstrates the relationship between Uchimura’s biblical commentary and his own early experience.

These lectures did not utilize the sophisticated techniques of biblical analysis that had developed in other parts of the world during Uchimura’s career. Instead, Uchimura made the Bible come to life by emphasizing the experience of biblical characters as they applied their faith to the world in which they lived. As part of his technique, Uchimura referred to his own experience in a way that led members of his audience to apply the words to their own experience. The detailed reference to his lectures that follows shows how he used the story of Job to represent the toils that befall one who tries to live his faith. The examination of four of the issues that Paul takes up in his Romans introduces readers to the problems that accompany taking on a new worldview and how to handle resultant questions when the new point of view brings one into conflict with society’s assumptions. Finally, an examination of Jesus’ appearance before Pilate relates what happened when Jesus’ new teaching brought him as a defendant before the majesty of the Roman Empire.

The choice of these selections is my own. They simply summarize a few of the many lectures that Uchimura delivered on these great books. I have chosen these particular selections because they reflect his position on issues that greatly affect those who dare to become Christians outside established Christian societies. The Book of Job deals with the misfortunes that descend upon a wealthy, productive, and pious man who pleases God greatly. Satan questions God’s confidence in his loyal servant. He points out that with many goods and a flourishing family Job has little reason to be other than devout. God agrees to test Job, first taking from him his possessions, his family, and then his own health. Finally, Job is reduced to scratching himself with a potsherd as he sits “among the ashes” (2:8).

Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Sophar, visit to discuss the cause of Job’s woes. Their lengthy discourses assume that Job has sinned and that confession will right him before God. Job remains convinced of his innocence but slowly withers before the onslaught of his visitors’ rhetoric. This encounter with his three “friends” forms the core of the book.

Most authorities consider the climax to come at Job 19:25, where Job, having finally pleaded with his friends for compassion, dreams that a description of his case is chiselled in stone to inform succeeding generations of his innocence. At this point, he suddenly discovers and puts into words the conviction that the King James version translates as “but as for me, I know that my redeemer liveth.” Although the New English Bible translates this as “but in my heart I know that my vindicator lives,” it is the old form that inspired centuries of Christians and continues to live through Handel’s setting in the Messiah. The concept of a redeemer is considered a prophecy of Christ’s advent.

This conviction of a means to get his message across to God enables Job to take the offensive. When he has roundly beaten them, a fourth, the young Elihu, steps up to argue God’s omnipotence. At this point, God himself intervenes and brings Job to an admission of his human limitations and prideful self-assertion. In Chapter 42, God then reprimands the three friends for misrepresenting him and restores Job to his former prosperity. God thus vindicates Job and asks him to pray for his friends. In the story of Job, the compilers of the Old Testament found a powerful statement of faith vindicated.

The following pages summarize Uchimura’s discussion of this text. Job’s concern over why misfortune visits the good, Uchimura begins, is not a mere philosophical exercise. It descends on him, and he has no choice but to live through it. People do not understand Job because they do not read it as experience. God never answers Job’s questions; this is surprising. But Job doesn’t mind. This is more surprising. His questions are not answered, yet through the experience itself he comes to know God, and this removes the need for other answers. Christians today must live through a similar experience. Whether such a man as Job actually existed one does not know, but the realism of the text makes one believe that it reflects facts.

The discussion between God and Satan makes us wonder whether all calamities come from God. God does initiate all things, even illness, that otherwise appear to be caused by nature. Only God knows why he acts this way.

In all, by the time that he sits among the ashes, Job has met six misfortunes, and the Middle Eastern way of thought would make one anticipate that there would be a total of seven. The seventh is the spiritual separation from his close friends, who come to counsel him. He feels their estrangement, and this leads to the lament in which he curses the day of his birth.

Job’s friends appear with their advice just as Job feels so abandoned. As a typical conservative, Eliphaz urges Job to do better in his attempt to live the Jewish law. Eliphaz does not realize that troubles plague Job so that he may escape this legalist attitude. If bad plagues only evil people, then Job must be bad, so Eliphaz exhorts him to renewed faith and outlines the benefits of God’s grace.

This situation may be restated in contemporary terms in this way. Job is a churchman suspected by others in the church of sins that he refuses to admit. The three friends are like a church committee formed by a minister, a theologian, and a concerned layman. Why, they ask, does Job not own up? He believes that misfortune does not always follow sin. Neither the three nor Job himself knows that this misfortune results from God’s attempt to test him. We should learn from this not to judge a man by the misfortunes that hit him but to judge the misfortunes by the character of the man’s response to them.
Job reproves Eliphaz for his lack of understanding, something all too common.

> Orthodoxy determines upon a set body of truth as a creed. This is an ideal situation if these truths are received and believed in the correct sense; such orthodoxy should be esteemed. But if succeeding generations accept without question and without reference to experience this body of truth as a hard and fast doctrine; if they pride themselves on the purity of their belief and force it upon others; if they use it to criticize others; if they dismiss as faithless and wrongdoing sinners those whose faith and actions go contrary to their own creed; this is what is usually called “orthodoxy.”

The second of the friends, Bildad, shares Eliphaz’s lack of human understanding. Bildad resembles a young theologian “who without intimate knowledge of his friend’s feelings attempts to impose his theology onto the friend, all the while priding himself on the purity of his own position. His words sound like a repetition of his notes taken from the ready-made doctrine he learned in seminary.” Bildad then invokes numerous authorities and precedents like a precocious student. He appeals to doctrine with no true love for Job. Job points out the absurdities of Bildad’s position. He does the same with Zophar. In these replies, Job gropes for an understanding of God’s love and the possibility of resurrection that will slowly lead to new faith.

In the second round of discussion, Eliphaz again links misfortune with evil deeds. He clearly defies life’s teaching that evil persons often live quite happy lives and die in peace, while the faithful frequently die in pain and fear, God’s necessary means to open humans’ spiritual eyes. Job criticizes the comfort offered by his friends. He talks of the word comfort as in the sense of the Japanese nagusame, which means the temporary relief from suffering offered by ignoring it. In contrast, the English word comfort used to translate the same original means to give strength through the mutual presence of friends in faith. Job, completely deserted by his friends in spite of their attempt to win him over, begins for the first time to sense his true relation to God.

Bildad’s second attack on Job displays his ability at logic and rhetoric to describe what Bildad considers Job’s defection. Finally, he hits the mark, for in Chapter 19 Job is reduced to seek pity from him and the others. Then something happens to Job. He looks at his assailants and turns to words of affirmation. He is led to seek a redeemer by “the natural action of his spirit. Not only he but anyone who in his circumstances does not give up the search for light finally comes to the same conclusion. To consider this not as special revelation but a natural need of man puts no special demands on our credulity. That so many among the Christians today share with Job faith in the second coming and resurrection shows that it answers a basic human need. The faithful ... seek only that which wells up from within their souls and at the same time is revealed by God.”

The affirmation that Job knows his redeemer lives is the climax of the book. To this point, Job, through his numerous sufferings, has accumulated the spiritual experience that enables him now to shift quickly to the strong faith in an intercessor who will speak to God on his behalf. All humans must move through such personal traumas to their own individual faith.

> [It] is basically personal; it is not social, national, or racial. Job suffered alone, discovered his redeemer alone, and finally came to say, “I know ... ” Everybody must be like Job. We do not get our knowledge of Christ in company with the rest of men; we know him individually. Today’s individual does not try to know God alone but in company with society, with the nation, and with all the nations of the world. This is a great error. It is because they start with such a mistaken view that there are now so many Christians of shallow faith.

Zophar, not recognizing the change in Job, continues. Job starts to express his love for those who have persecuted him. They continue to accuse him through a third whole cycle of debate, followed by a last attempt by the youthful Elihu. He enters the dispute when he recognizes that his elders have failed. But Job wants to address God. His request is granted, for the “author of Job is a poet ... as well as an expert in the essential problems of spirituality. Therefore in the end he shows God to Job, ... and a great sense of satisfaction” comes over Job. When God appears, he challenges Job to equal him, and Job recognizes God’s sovereignty. It is easy to espouse such a relation in words but difficult to believe it. Once one can believe in God’s power, then he or she can relax and ask in honesty that “Thy will be done.”

Although Job’s early and later prosperity seem similar on the surface, there is a difference. At first, Job thought that he prospered because he was good; in the end, he found himself wealthy in spite of his evil. “The unbeliever considers the possession of wealth to be a right bestowed by his virtue; as a result, when he has little he feels great dissatisfaction. But the believer is satisfied with little because he believes that everything results not from his labor but from God’s benevolence.”

As this summary of Uchimura’s interpretation indicates, he treated Job as a work of heuristic artistry – written with the intent to inform humans about their relationship with God – but also as great literature. Uchimura vacillates between an interpretation of the work as a mirror of his own experience and belles lettres. And he identifies with Job. In his diary for the day he gave the lecture on the end of Chapter 16, where Job first senses that there may be an intermediary, Uchimura wrote, “I felt as if I had become Job ... Tears welled up within my eyes, and I realized that many members of the audience were wiping their eyes. Mine was not the voice of an ecclesiastic or theologian. It was the voice of a human being. It was the voice of a human driven into a corner by bodily suffering and the unconcern of the church.” Less than a month later, right after the lecture on Chapter 19, where Job announces his belief in a redeemer, Uchimura became dizzy. The symptoms continued, and in his diary the next day he went on, “it is natural for this to happen when one has been discussing Job 19. One cannot say that he understands Job unless he has pushed himself to the point of collapse.”

Although in his discussion of the introduction of God into the final chapters Uchimura refers to the work as fiction, at other times he sees it as autobiography that makes the reader identify with the author. This is just the kind of work that Uchimura produced in his pioneering Consolations of a Christian. There his description of his friends’ lack of compassion pictures a despair like Job’s. The similarity ends in the final lectures on Job, where Uchimura, like his subject, expresses confident faith. To Uchimura, Job becomes Everyman but in particular Uchimura himself.

Those who heard the lectures on Job were greatly moved. A crowd of 800 jammed the hall for the climactic lecture on Chapter 19. Ishiwara tells us he went back to his lodgings afterward but could not settle down. In search of a quiet place to meditate, he climbed the steps of a nearby shrine, from which, absorbed in his thoughts, he looked out over Tokyo Bay. And then he bowed his head in a short but fervent prayer. Others had similar reactions. The lectures appeared in book form in 1922 and were reprinted four times before Uchimura died. Since the Second World War, they have appeared in paperback and in the new editions of the Complete Works.

That so many of the deshi responded in this way attests to Uchimura’s ability to make them realize the estrangement from their own society that conversion had entailed. Conversion itself could be seen as a test devised by God to challenge their resolve. His own emotion at the pivotal moment in the story also demonstrated why at times Uchimura felt that conversion to Christianity had come at tremendous spiritual cost. It was easy to conclude that all Christians, but particularly Japanese Christians, replicated in their own experience that of Job.

During a four-week rest after the climactic lecture, Uchimura decided to skip the later debates between Job and his friends until God’s appearance in Chapter 38. This agreed with his general interpretation of Chapter 29 as the climax. As Uchimura tied together the loose ends of the lectures on Job, he began an even bigger project, the one that many would consider his greatest work. This was his mammoth commentary on the Letter to the Romans. He had the Bible Society bind special editions of Romans with blank pieces of paper interspersed between pages of the text to facilitate taking notes. He moved from identifying the experience of all Christians as similar to Job’s to analyzing how Paul dealt with his own experience when he tried to link his new faith to that into which he had been born. Uchimura identified himself with Paul, as he would later express it, with a parallel between Paul’s rejection by the synagogue in Ephesus and Uchimura’s rejection by the religious establishment at the YMCA. Both Paul and Uchimura had, as a result, he went on, changed their emphasis from working with other members of the faith to appealing to the “Gentiles” in secular surroundings.

Both Uchimura and his listeners anticipated great things from the lectures born of these sentiments. Uchimura began them in January 1921 and continued each Sunday for twenty-two months until October 1923. Only illness and summer holidays led him to break the succession. For the first half of the series, Seisho no Kenkyû published the lectures as recorded by the amanuensis. For the remainder of the sixty lectures, Seisho no Kenkyû carried Uchimura’s own notes along with the text provided by the amanuensis. This care reflected the concern that Uchimura shared with the deshi that the total experience should be preserved for posterity.

The Letter to the Romans occupies a pivotal place in the New Testament and is located right after the four Gospels and the Book of Acts. Paul was the greatest among the apostles, working with both Gentiles and those who, like him, had been born Jewish. His Letter to the Romans sets forth what he considered the core of his belief and its relation to the Judaism from which it had developed. Ever since his dramatic conversion, Paul had worked to reconcile his old understanding of religion to his new belief that Jesus had been the Christ prophesied in the Old Testament. In the process, Paul first wrestled with the implications of this revelation within himself and then proclaimed his resultant conviction to others.

His conclusions aligned him with one of the two major interpretations of Jesus’ significance. If Jesus had come as the Christ out of the Jewish tradition and spoke only to the Jews, then everything that he proclaimed was true only for those who, like himself and Paul, had been born Jews. If, on the other hand, his message applied to all people everywhere, then the Jews formed a very small part of the total to whom Jesus addressed his words. Paul led those who favoured the second interpretation and himself addressed, as he frequently said, Gentile and Jew alike. Romans summarizes the results of twenty years of thought on this basic problem in a manner so comprehensive that the editors of the New English Bible of 1970 call the first half of it “The Gospel According to Paul.” It is the “most systematic and complete, as well as the weightiest,” of the letters identified as his.

Paul wrote to the Romans from what is now Turkey. He tells us that he plans a trip to Rome to visit the Christians there but in the meantime will content himself with a letter to them. The contents of his letter make it clear that he addresses a congregation where the influence of Jewish Christians is strong. The members find themselves wondering about the relations between their old customs and their new convictions. The first eight chapters, Paul’s “gospel,” deal with the plan kept secret for long generations but now revealed in Jesus Christ for the salvation of all nations and the relation of this plan to the moral and cultic “law.” This was the collection of stipulations by which Jews regulated lives in the faith so that punctilious observance would save them and by extension their whole people. Paul points out that the law cannot “save” or “justify” humans; only faith can do that, faith that the power of God through Jesus can make us the sort of persons worthy of salvation. It will help us to be the kind of individuals that the law was supposed to produce but could not. He ends Chapter 8 with a ringing declaration of his own conviction that “nothing in all creation ... can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Paul then turns in Chapters 9-11 to discuss Israel, the society of which the individual Jews are the constituent parts and in which the Jews as a people are considered to be God’s elect. Paul reinterprets the concept of the elect to mean not those who are physical descendents of Abraham, regarded as the founder of the Jewish people, but those who live by the true spirit of God. Although he shows deep concern for the Jews, he believes that they have not lived up to God’s holy calling. God is saving Gentiles so that the Jews may observe what is happening and themselves gain the same spirit as those converted Gentiles. Although Paul himself feels as a result that in his experience he has passed beyond the Jews, he concerns himself for them as all individuals care for family members or their society and shows his fellows how they can follow God’s lead.

Paul then passes on to his last major topic, the Christian life – how to live in the new understanding of existence that God has introduced through Christ. He enjoins his readers to submit to the civil authorities and points out the many good things that the Roman government was doing. This closes the major part of the letter that has informed the Jewish Christians how their new faith relates to the old, how it affects their relationships with their kinship groups as well as Gentile society, and how they should act with each other and strangers. It trumpets Paul’s own convictions.

The following four summaries of portions in Uchimura’s Romans demonstrate his interpretation on a number of key points. The longest section deals with Paul’s discussion in Chapter 3 of how converts relate the morality of their new faith to the rules with which they grew up and still govern the lives of their families and friends. Later Uchimura uses Paul’s Chapter 8 to answer how the convert, without the support of family and tradition, learns how to implement the new faith. Uchimura concludes that one not brought up in the Christian tradition can do this only through Bible study. When the converts despair about the immorality of the world around them, Uchimura relates Paul’s lament over Israel’s defection from God in Chapter 9 to Taishô Japan. And, finally, he refers to Paul’s advocacy in Chapter 13 of submission to government authority. Uchimura asks if there can be no exceptions to this rule.

Each of these questions plagues converts as they grow into their faith. Uchimura deals with them apparently incidentally as he proceeds with his deliberate explication of the text phrase by phrase. His listeners, raised in a tradition that applied the same method to traditional Confucian texts, could understand the relevance of the important passages to their own lives.

These excerpts come from the transcriptions of Azegami Kenzô. For the latter half of the series, when Uchimura’s own lecture notes were published along with Azegami’s version, comparison of the two indicates that, as he lectured, Uchimura frequently deviated from what he had planned to say. Although his notes are more controlled and scholarly, it is what he said with its rhetorical emphasis that made the immediate impact on his listeners and remains the most compelling. Therefore, I take quotations from Azegami’s transcripts.

In each excerpt from Azegami, phrases in quotation marks translate the sense of the original with some phrases in which Uchimura has used highly allusive Chinese characters omitted. Although these expressions enhance the impact in the original, they cannot be translated without repetition. It is therefore more in the interest of the reader’s understanding to omit them, attempting by other devices to approximate in English the spirit of the original.

The first selection is the latter half of the lecture “Rippô no nôryoku” (The Power of the Law), lecture sixteen. It deals with Romans 3:19-20, which include the phrase “now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced.” Uchimura begins as follows.

> “Law” means “morals” [dôtoku]. What Paul says here about “law” refers in a broad sense to the imperatives of morals. Since Paul was brought up under the law of Moses and since the gospel of Christ was born out of Judea to replace the law of Moses, Paul discussed the law of Moses alone, but his thesis applies to all moral laws ... Heathen countries of course have moral laws. In some societies they are set down as written precepts or teachings, while members of other societies keep them unwritten as an instinctual realization of their corporate conscience. And no individual in any society is justified by those morals. To generalize, no one can be justified before God by moral actions and can therefore in the true sense be saved. That is because man cannot be morally perfect. Man knows his sins through morals, [since] they were given by God to man “so that ... the whole world may be held accountable to God” [3:19]. This is not to denigrate morals but on the contrary to make clear their true nature and define their value. We Japanese are a people brought up encased in a cavern of morals ... The most pervasive element of a society is its moral atmosphere. (This is not to say that our race is morally superior. It is said in the same sense that one says that the peoples of Europe and America who have such a pervasive religious atmosphere are not necessarily religiously superior.) Thus the yardstick of judgement regarding all things is in the main moral laws. Loyalty, filial piety, benevolence and justice [the four Confucian virtues, chû, kô, jin, gi] are the keynotes of home and school education. This is proof that these morals – even though not always followed – are the best part of our society.

> But what about the proposition that “morals demonstrate man’s sin but do not save him”? It is unnecessary to point out that this is a revolutionary proposition. If one accepts it, the home education based on morals and the school and social education that aims to save man through morals will result in nothing and will crumble away like a house without a foundation. To say that morals are unnecessary is a proposal for spiritual revolution against a society based on morals. It attempts to show that morals are not the salvation of the world. They do not reform from the ground up the individuals and their society based on morals. Nor do they build anew a basis of faith. If these words are true, Paul poses a grave problem for individuals and societies that rest upon a moral base, a problem that cannot be lightly ignored. But the Christian contention is very clear and leaves little ground for doubt. One scholar has said, “Christianity alone is a religion that teaches that man is not saved by morals.” This is true, but the superior morals of Christianity are byproducts and not in any way its core. Since man cannot be saved by morals, the gospel that can save men cannot in any way be based on morals. Individuals cannot become morally perfect, so their actions cannot justify them before God. The gospel has salvation as its central message, and so this truth must be its strongest contention. It is because of just this message that Paul encountered much persecution and slander. His enemies shadowed him about and tried covertly and openly to undermine his teaching. But he overcame all difficulties and continued his preaching. Even though the darkness tried to overcome the light, the light gradually increased in brilliance.

> To save men – yes, for that very reason – he constantly lighted spiritual torches. One theologian has said, “Paul changed the straightforward teaching of Christ into complicated theological doctrine. If he had not lived, Christianity would probably have remained a beautiful moral teaching that had arisen in the hills of Judea.” I wonder if that is really so. We do not have the time for a lengthy discussion here. But if we look at it as simple human experience, we cannot but recognize Paul’s assertion to be living fact. Morals are holy and right. But we discover when we try to implement them the impossibility of our task and acutely feel our own lack of rectitude judged by their standards. Although the Ten Commandments are in fact perfect moral laws, they cannot save mankind; on the contrary, judged by them, individuals come to know that moral actions cannot justify them. What attacks us at this time is the anguish of sin. It is a spiritual groaning that, as if bubbling up from our inner depths, encourages us to purify ourselves though we cannot succeed. We cannot calm this sensation with some simple rationalization. What are we to do when we have firmly determined to lead a pure and moral life but at the same time behold so clearly our moral inability? The distance between determination and reality, between ideal and actuality, is as great as that between the stars that twinkle in the heavens. Morals never lead man to the joy of salvation. To the extent that moral laws are elevated, they make individuals feel their inability to follow them. Thus it is a very clear demonstration that moral actions cannot save mankind. Then what is the use of morals? We are told that it resides in their ability to make man aware of his sin.

> Paul said that “through the law comes the knowledge of sin” [3:20]. Of course, we should not overlook the one aspect of morals that sets standards for the interaction between individuals. But we must fully recognize that morals mainly exist to make people recognize their own sin. There are people who leave Christianity as impossibly difficult after, in their attempt to study it, they first read the Sermon on the Mount and then, struck by its beauty, try to implement it in their daily life but find they cannot. This is because they have mistakenly regarded Christianity too simply as an ethical teaching. While the Sermon on the Mount as heaven’s morality points out the way that those who have been saved should follow, it also points out to those who read it their own sin ... Thus, while morals have great power to inform us of our sin, they lack any power to save us. The strength and the weakness of morals are here clearly set forth. Morals are very strong in making men out to be sinners but in other respects have no power. This claim that Paul put forth with such strength becomes a truth clear as the light of day when seen through the experience of men who have sincerely tried to implement morals ... People who look at morals superficially and for their externals alone and then make themselves quite nonchalantly out to be moralists are too flippant, too inconstant, and absolutely unable to discuss the basic problems of human beings. We should consider Japan’s experience in education over the past decades. Everyone now recognizes the failure of the Meiji and Taishô moral education that rested upon loyalty and patriotism. As a result, it appears that education is at a standstill groping about for new ideas.

> No people have received as completely worked out an ethical indoctrination as the contemporary Japanese ... What has resulted? Is not the nation about to drown in the slops of corruption, unrighteousness and violence? What about the competition between juvenile delinquents and adolescent delinquents or the preponderance of mature delinquents and aged delinquents? In the contemporary world, the Earth is swept clear of virtue, and morality conceals itself. Our society in fact stands on the brink of moral bankruptcy. Ah! Are these the results of all that moral cultivation? Yes! These are the results of all that moral cultivation. Morals do not have the power to do what they propose. Cultivation based on morals alone cannot make men avoid evil. Moral education makes people aware of their own sin and at the same time enables them to recognize other people’s sin. The present situation wherein we recognize quite well our own evil as well as devote ourselves to ferret out the evil of others amply demonstrates the nature of moral cultivation and its results. Moral cultivation does not make people any more moral but simply makes them more keen in their moral criticism of themselves and others. Just as Paul said, the law produces a consciousness of sin. When viewed against the standards of ethics and morals, all the world is adjudged sinful before God. Not one person can be justified by observance of the law. But can people go no further than this? It is true that people can go no further as far as morals are concerned. To put it another way, mankind’s plan to be saved through morals can go no further. But mankind’s blind alley is not God’s blind alley. God opens up a whole game plan for people’s salvation. In the following verses, “God’s justice independent of the law” appears.

> This is the way of faith. Thus we who have been stifled by the law are resurrected by faith. Those who have not been justified by the law are justified by faith. Here salvation awaits us, and the dew of joy bathes our spirits.

In this passage, Uchimura analyzed Paul’s intent and how his words reflect his own society. Uchimura then went on to examine the applicability of the words to contemporary Japanese society. He discussed how one learns to govern his or her life in a society hostile to Christianity by reference to Paul. In his Chapter 8, Paul talks of grace working within humans to bring God and humans together. Although this sounds very theoretical, far removed from everyday concerns, Uchimura concluded, it is not. The Bible remains popular precisely because it deals with our most real preoccupations.

> The Bible and in particular Romans solve the problems of just action in human society ... But if one pursues the problem of just action by the individual, one ends with the question of how to become justified before God. When people by some means become justified before God, then for the first time they can act justly, and those who can act justly as individuals for the first time can act justly in company with other people. Therefore, if one asks how justice can be done in human society, the problem at its most basic becomes how can man be justified before God? As a result, the problem of peace between individuals becomes in essence the problem of peace between God and people. The problem of justice between people becomes the problem of justice between God and individuals. Those nurtured in Christian societies have a sense of God’s identification with men worked into their backgrounds, whether they consciously act in accordance with these teachings or not ... Who can say that the Bible that has for so many years nourished the peoples of Europe and America is not even now ruling their emotions and spirits? What about their ancestors? What about their traditions? Of course, one cannot say that they do not think about their national interests, but it is an undeniable fact that they also have a great and deep sense of public spiritedness ... The central concerns of the Bible are motivating the deepest recesses of their spirits. In a sense, the Bible is ruling them ... Someone has said, “In the 2,600 years since the Prophet Isaiah foretold peace, mankind has not stopped fighting, but it has maintained the hope and ideal to give up fighting.” Peace is in fact a problem of the Bible. The spirit of the Bible will continue until peace is realized ...
> Therefore, everyone must study it with great enthusiasm.

In this passage on Romans 8, we witness one of the core elements of Uchimura’s interpretation. In the first passage, where Uchimura uses succeeding dependent clauses followed by conclusions (“if ... then”), he echoes the rhetoric of classical Chinese that has informed the study of ethics in Northeast Asia for centuries. In the following paragraph, he turns to the similar effect that the cadences of the Bible have exercised over leaders nurtured in the Christian tradition. As he spoke, world leaders at the Washington Conference were forcing the Japanese to accept limitations on their territorial ambitions. Uchimura points out that the Western negotiators act from the basis of public good to implement Isaiah’s prophecy of peace. Members of Uchimura’s audience would have recognized this conviction as necessary if Japan was to take its place among the advanced nations.

Two months later Uchimura had moved on to Chapter 9. Here Paul expresses his concern about the separation from his fellow Jews induced by his conversion. Paul stresses that God will keep his word to save the descendants of Abraham but interprets the term “descendants” to mean those who inherit Abraham’s faith rather than his blood. By these words, Paul opens up the possibility that all peoples may share in the special status that Jews thought reserved for them.

In his commentary, Uchimura says that he also worried about his fellow Japanese when he was converted. “All true patriots,” he goes on, “have the same concern for their fellows ... Love of God naturally leads to love of countrymen and then of all people ... Our own fellows now consider no one but themselves and reject Christ, but we are told that God will by some means save them also. Therefore, we sow seeds in tears convinced that we shall reap in joy. We know that our race in the past has produced excellent religious leaders and believers. As Paul counts up the virtues of his fellows, so we count up those of our friends.”

Two months later Uchimura had moved on to consider Romans 13:1-7, where Paul enjoins Christians to submit to government authority. Is Paul correct in all cases, Uchimura asks, when he advises us to obey the state?

> Christians are men of peace. They dislike revolutions, riots and insurrections. One does not hear of true Christians who have disrupted the social order or rebelled against the state ... That the peoples of America and Europe engage in frequent ... wars while calling themselves Christians reflects the height of hypocrisy. Their assertion of one philosophy as they follow another introduces another problem. If a government becomes very corrupt and the clear enemy of the people, if one’s own country becomes a despotic state and languishes under tyranny, what then? In this case, should the citizens not raise the banner of revolution and independence in opposition? Look at the English Revolution of Cromwell, the War of Independence of Prince William of Orange in the Netherlands, and the American War of Independence of George Washington. Each of these revolts ... opposed unrestrained unrighteousness in the cause of righteousness and love. As a result, should these not be recognized as righteous wars, something in which Christians would naturally take part? Such an act is indeed rebellion, but is it not such that it can be encouraged, or at least approved, by Christians? Such examples are very rare. And to affirm revolt in such exceptional cases is not to say that it is right in more ordinary circumstances. Paul here instructs Christians in their normal attitudes and expresses the basic principle that one should generally submit to the political authorities. But what of such exceptional circumstances as those mentioned above? If one looks at certain aspects of his spirit, and in particular if one appeals to the spirit of the Lord Jesus, I believe one can in general know what is best.

> That is, when a government abuses its authority so that everyone suffers, Christians should rely on peaceful measures alone. First they should protest to those in authority with humility and conciliation. They should protest time and again with measures that do not exceed peaceful expression. They must pray for success with unflagging spirits. But if they fail, they must not appeal to arms. They must limit themselves to peaceful means and entrust the outcome entirely to the hands of the Almighty. Now what should we think about the Japanese government? We should decry its many faults, but we must recognize that it is a relatively good government. Most Japanese who return home from travel abroad agree with this. Not a few foreigners resident in Japan also agree. We enjoy safety for our lives and property, freedom of faith, and to an extent freedom of thought. Within this country, we can study the gospel and proclaim it in peace. If Paul were to be born in contemporary Japan, he would probably praise the Japanese government for the freedom and conveniences it accords to the propagation of the gospel.

Uchimura thus urged his listeners to consider the relative morality of the Japanese government, even as he gave them a clear imperative that in extreme cases they should oppose their own government. Although they limited their actions to words, some of the leading opponents of the government’s actions in the Pacific War came from among those who heard Uchimura speak that day. Halfway around the world in Switzerland, the theologian Karl Barth had wrestled a few years earlier with the same problem as he heard the cannonades of the First World War on the other side of the Swiss border.

These summaries of how Uchimura treated key portions of Romans open the way to a more thorough comparison of his conclusions to those of Barth. Uchimura knew of Barth, and it is highly likely that Barth had read Uchimura’s How I Became a Christian. In the same way that Barth exercised great influence over Christian thinkers in countries where most of the people considered themselves Christian, Uchimura emphasized Paul’s relevance for those who themselves had made the leap of faith into Christian belief. Uchimura’s position began with an understanding of the man Jesus, and it was to this subject that he turned in his final great series of lectures. Uchimura described the life of Jesus in seventy-four lectures. The first fortysix dealt with Jesus’ early life and teaching. They were delivered between October 1922, the week after the final lecture on Romans, and June 1924 and appeared in print the following year as Gariraya no michi (The Galilean Way). The final thirty cover the last five days of Jesus’ life: his triumphal entry into Jerusalem and the conflict with religious authorities that led to his crucifixion. Uchimura delivered them between February 1925 and March 1926 and published them in 1928 as Jûjika no michi (The Via Dolorosa). Together they form commentaries on the most important elements of the four Gospels.

Uchimura introduced what later became these two volumes as simple tools to assist in the understanding of the Gospels. Of them, he placed primary reliance on Matthew, for it, he believed, gives the reader the greatest detail on the teaching that Uchimura considered Jesus’ main task. Uchimura did not concern himself with the various differences in the four accounts or try to “harmonize” the Gospels, for, as he had said almost twenty years earlier, they were written as evangelizing instruments, not as historical documents. It was the clear intent of the works together rather than their individual differences that should attract the student’s attention. Jesus is reported, for instance, to have “cleansed” the temple at two times in his career, driving out the peddlers who sold animals for sacrifice and coins for offering. The Gospel According to St. John says that this happened at the beginning of his career, while the other three say that it happened at the end. “We cannot be sure that he did it twice or once. Yet it does no harm to think that he did it twice.” Books written as guides to faith need not meet the same standards as works of history.

With this attitude toward the harmonization of the Gospels, certainly the most elementary task in the Western scientific approach, it is not surprising that Uchimura ignored so many other elements of that method. The most prolific among the professional students of Uchimura, Yamamoto Taijirô, has pointed out that Uchimura referred hardly at all to the problems “of original sources, authorship, special vocabulary and style, and similarity between” the Gospels. He had interest in these problems but did not inject them into his lectures. “He gives the impression that he completely overlooks the problems of higher and lower criticism,” believing that he had no time for these “hobbies.” Even within Matthew he makes no reference to Chapters 1-2 or 11-20. He does not deal with Christ’s lineage, virginal conception, birthday, youth, and visitation to the temple, though he covered these topics elsewhere. His omissions indicate that he wanted at this point “to demonstrate through Christ’s teachings and works that he was the savior as both the son of God and the son of man, ... to write an ethical and spiritual inner biography. This is demonstrated by his use of fifteen lectures, one-fifth of the total, for the Sermon on the Mount.”

Yamamoto’s analysis captures the essence of Uchimura’s intent. Uchimura did not want to evaluate the works scientifically but hoped to present the image of “a very special, and yet in many ways very ordinary, man.” It is a great mistake, Uchimura pointed out, to consider Jesus particularly different. He was not; he did not come to cause revolt, but revolt followed because he was so thoroughly human and humane. He spoke as a simple human being and so called forth defensive reactions against himself. Many people consider the Sermon on the Mount the core of his teaching. They err, for the last three chapters of Matthew that deal with his betrayal, crucifixion, and resurrection form its core.
In the spirit of this interpretation by Uchimura, the following excerpt presents a virtually complete translation of lecture twenty-five as it appears in The Via Dolorosa.

> Lecture 25: Christ before Pilate Matthew 27:11-26; Mark 14:1-15; Luke 23:1-25; John 18:28-40; 19:1-16 The high priest and the elders of the people sentenced Jesus to death, bound him and led him to Pontius Pilate, the governor from Rome. That was because the church authorities did not have the authority to execute the death penalty but had to appeal to the governor ( John 18:31). And Jesus standing before Pilate felt much more at peace than he had felt before Caiaphas. Between him and the high priest there was nothing but ill will. The high priest and the others had known that any statement on his own behalf was worthless. But none of these feelings existed with Pilate. There was neither understanding nor sympathy between them. At the same time, there was no ill will. Whereas Caiaphas had been his foe, Pilate was simply disinterested. Caiaphas was a religionist, and Pilate was an official. And as regards their dislike for men of faith, religionists go much beyond officials. Men of faith cannot hope for understanding or sympathy from officials, but they will not find in them the ill will and animosity which religionists seem to harbor toward them. Pilate was much more tolerant of Jesus than Caiaphas. Jesus stood before Pilate. Pilate asked Jesus, “are you the king of the Jews?” That is to say, “are you the Christ of the Jews about whom I have heard?” When Pilate first met Jesus, he was surprised. He had heard about the king of the Jews, and he expected someone with the air and dignity of a king, but when he met this man, he was a commoner from Galilee and had none of the marks of a king about him. When he realized that this was the “king of the Jews” about whom he had heard, Pilate probably felt relieved and perhaps could hardly stifle a chuckle.

> And the first thing that came into his mind was that this man was certainly no criminal who deserved death. Therefore, Pilate cast about for some way to release Jesus. He immediately understood that the Jews “had brought Jesus before him out of malice” (Matthew 27:18). Therefore, as an official, there was no way that he could pass a death sentence on Jesus. He first planned to release Jesus by using the precedent to release at the Passover one prisoner at the request of the people. But since the people followed the lead of the high priest, they requested that the murderer Barrabas be released and shouted that Jesus be crucified, so that this plan did not work. At this point, Pilate devised another plan. Because he knew that Jesus was a Galilean, Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, the magistrate over Galilee who happened at that time to be in Jerusalem. By this means, Pilate planned to have Herod deal with this Jesus of Nazareth, who came within Herod’s jurisdiction. But as soon as Herod saw Jesus and Jesus did not comply with Herod’s request that he perform a miracle, Herod returned Jesus to Pilate. At this point, Pilate as his third and final device washed his hands before the multitude and said, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man. See ye to it.” By thus clearly proclaiming Jesus’ innocence, he hoped to make the crowd relent and prevent a riot. But such weak methods had no chance of success, and the crowd shouted ever louder, “Crucify him! Crucify him! His blood be on us and on our children.” Seeing that his stratagems were to no avail, the Governor Pilate bowed to the will of the crowd, had Jesus whipped and ordered that he be crucified, and then handed him over to the mob. The pathetic and weak-willed politician Pilate lacked the courage to protect innocence.

> Pilate’s attitude is at the same time blameworthy and pitiable. He was an ordinary official of the Roman government. And most officials were ordinary men. There was no reason to expect that he would have the light to recognize the holy nature of Jesus, and he lacked either the courage or the fidelity to discard his own life in the ends of justice. His first hope was to protect his own safety, next the trust of his superiors and finally the confidence of the crowd. Although he wanted to be fair, his impartiality extended only to the extent that it did not endanger the safety of his jurisdiction. Pilate clearly recognized Jesus’ innocence, but he did not have the courage to proclaim this conviction if it might cost him the confidence of the people. When he was told by the mob, “if you let this man go, you are no friend of Caesar; any man who claims to be a king is defying Caesar” (John 19:12), he recognized the danger of his position. His superiors would say that all that was at stake was the life of one country bumpkin, and there was no likelihood that a disturbance would break out among the people ... just because his life was sacrificed. Seeing things in this light, Pilate ignored his conscience, pronounced a death sentence on the guiltless Jesus and handed him over to his enemies. And the tolerant Jesus, even at this point, once again forgot himself and sympathized with Pilate. Instead of the complete silence he had maintained before the priests and others, he said a great deal to Pilate. John 18:28 to 19:14 tells us what transpired. Pilate asked him, “you know that I have authority to release you, and I have authority to crucify you.”

> Jesus replied, “you would have no authority at all over me, if it had not been granted you from above; and therefore the deeper guilt lies with the man who handed me over to you.” With this Jesus clearly indicated the degree of Pilate’s responsibility for Jesus’ own death. Jesus did not deny that Pilate had responsibility but stated that the priests and others had a higher responsibility. Even though they were the ones who had sentenced him to death, he did not assign them a greater responsibility than they in fact had. Before Pilate could defend his own actions, Jesus defended them for him. But Jesus expected nothing from the official Pilate, who put his own safety above all else. Jesus knew well that there was no reason to expect perfect impartiality from him. Officials are officials; though they are not at all useless, they cannot be depended upon in matters regarding God or justice; this is the same now as in the past, in the East as well as in the West. Experience proves the error of trusting officials regarding matters of righteousness because the government has appointed them as civil servants. Pilate was a fortunate official ... There were many other officials of his category within the broad Roman Empire. But their names have been entirely forgotten, and only Pilate’s name lives throughout history. At the same time, he was also an unfortunate official. He was put in the position of pronouncing a death sentence upon the son of God. Even an outstanding official would have had great difficulty in fulfilling his responsibility. It was very similar to President Coolidge’s position when in 1924 the United States Congress passed the Anti-Japanese Law.

> For Coolidge to sign was a sin; if he did not sign, his own and his people’s obvious ineptitude would be apparent; he hesitated over his decision and finally took the easy way out. One criticizes his ineffective will and weak solution but at the same time sympathizes with him. Pilate was a good official. Government officials, whether prime minister or members of the Diet, the lowest civil servants or officials: 999 out of 1,000 resemble Pilate. They do not know God; they do not understand Christ; though they mouth words like justice and impartiality, they lack the courage of a child to implement them. One can understand as a result how foolish it is to depend upon politicians to spread the gospel or expand its influence. The many ecclesiastics who seek assistance for evangelism from the Pilate who sentenced Christ to death or who run to officials to help expand their influence should consider what they are doing. It was not Christ before Pilate, but Pilate before Christ. Pilate did not judge Christ; Christ judged Pilate. Pilate, a symbol for all officials, was here judged by Christ. The famous painting of Munkácsy clearly pictures this. However good the written commentary, it cannot better explain this incident.

Uchimura thus ends his study of Jesus’ trial with reference to his high moral stance before the secular authorities who had condemned Jesus. Uchimura’s strictures against those in political authority, while generally apt, could not challenge in this form the authority of the Taishô state. Uchimura need not have feared the censors in the Japanese government, though the trial of Christ corroborated his distrust of all secular institutions. In addition to Uchimura’s biography of Jesus, a final selection demonstrates his allusive use of a Bible passage with specific connotations in his own life. It appears in his study on the book of Hosea, a series of ten lectures delivered in May and June 1928 as Uchimura ruminated on the half century since his baptism. Hosea is the greatest among the minor prophets, a man who, we are told, married a harlot, suffered from her infidelity, and then made of his own experience an allegory that likens the unfaithful wife’s relationship with her husband to Israel’s relationship with God.

In his introduction to the series, Uchimura says that a passage in Hosea once saved his life. It appears that this refers to the period after his divorce when he first read Hosea. In his lectures, Uchimura covers the passages that deal with Hosea’s unsuccessful marriage in number three, “Katei no fukô” (Domestic Misfortune).

God calls people, he begins, in different ways. Hosea was called through his marital life. The text says that God commanded him to take a harlot for a wife. We cannot accept this as literal. Hosea learned after the fact that he had chosen a bad woman. Then he realized in retrospect that this had been God’s call. “Hosea mistakenly married a harlot, for that reason experienced much suffering, endured slander, and only later realized that it had all occurred because of God’s intent.” Each of the children born to her seemed not to be his, so he gave each of them an unlucky name. There is no unhappiness in life like a “failure in marriage. Usually, it does not stop with the breakup of the home but extends to the breakup of life itself. It was undoubtedly particularly painful for someone as emotional and spiteful as Hosea. Failure in love has driven many young persons to death. Hosea also probably longed at this time after the grave. He did not know what kind of man the fickle woman Gomer was keeping. She did not think that when she ran through his heart with the sword of her indecency she was doing anything particularly wrong.” But God called Hosea to himself through the infidelity of his wife. Hosea understood why he suffered: that he was not alone, that his domestic misfortune simply reflected the social and ethical confusion of his time, that before he lamented his suffering he should bewail the problem of his nation, that “the main cause of social and ethical confusion is the spread of false religion ... In Hosea’s home, there had been misfortune because true faith had disappeared from Israel. The Holy Spirit showed this to him, and he well understood the lesson.”

Hosea also learned that the relationship of wife to husband is like the relationship of humans to God. When love disappears, the relationship ceases to exist: “apostasy is adultery, and Hosea learned through his wife’s adultery the depth and decadence of Israel’s sin when it deserted Jehovah to serve [the heathen god] Ba’al. Thus Hosea overcame his personal misfortune. He saw it as one part of national misfortune. Also, after he himself had experienced God’s grief, he had to rise on behalf of the holy name. Thus his misfortune became the opportunity for his call by God and his appearance as a prophet.”

Probably no one in the audience could have known when that lecture was delivered on 6 May 1928 the extent to which it reflected Uchimura’s own experience. It had been about forty-three years since his divorce and thirty-three years since Uchimura had used the allusive phrases from Hosea 2:14-16 to describe the spiritual wanderings that began after he left the Sapporo church and climaxed with his divorce. Since he had never mentioned the divorce in any of his writings, only Nitobe Inazô, Miyabe Kingo, Ebina Danjô, and a handful of other friends who remembered the circumstances could link the lecture to his own experience.

This was undoubtedly as Uchimura wanted it. Yet in reading his words, one can see how the heartbreak of his youthful divorce has become through his experience God’s handiwork. In the first place, Uchimura cannot accept as literal the statement that God told Hosea to marry a harlot. Certainly, one would not expect God to advise such a move, but given the use to which God puts the resultant union it seems possible. If one accepts the Uchimura interpretation that the text errs and Hosea found out only after marriage the proclivities of his wife, then the parallel with Kanzô’s own innocent betrothal is established. Because of his error, Hosea experiences the deep pain of “failure in marriage.” His wife’s acts deeply hurt Hosea, though he recognizes that she probably does not think she is “doing anything particularly wrong.” Throughout his misfortune, Hosea realizes that it results in part from the sin of his people. He overcomes this personal misfortune by linking his grief to the fate of his nation. This interpretation becomes “the opportunity for his call by God and his appearance as a prophet.”

The biographer can only list the coincidences mentioned above and take no conclusions from them, but the evidence intimates that in this passage Uchimura answered the critics of his youth. He says in his diary that he wants to discuss this book “once.” He said in How I Became a Christian that he was “allured by God into the wilderness” to become “a MAN first and then a PATRIOT.” In this passage, Uchimura sees that God used the divorce to this end. The unfortunate Take receives nothing but the recognition that she probably acted in good faith. Here, then, is the closest that one can come to the single most perplexing question about Kanzô as reflected in How I Became a Christian: why did he feel such guilt and use the metaphor of the vacuum to describe the whole period of study in America?

Little good would have been accomplished if more members of the congregation who heard the lecture had known his experience that informed it. They only knew that it was a fine exposition of a difficult text. Within a month, Uchimura would celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of his conversion, and within six months he would be embroiled in a controversy that ended with his death. At this point, he appears to have felt secure enough for the first time to intimate how the curse of Kanzô’s youth could finally be introduced into Uchimura’s creative work. As this lengthy series of passages demonstrates, the Bible research of Uchimura differs greatly from the enterprise that goes under the same name decades later in the societies where Christianity has flourished. The wealth of historical, linguistic, and archeological techniques based upon secular assumptions have produced a mass of information that goes far beyond what Uchimura, operating by himself and from a basis of faith alone, commanded or desired. His writing at the time appeared out of date to many of his colleagues learned in contemporary Western biblical studies. His close friend of thirty years, Uemura Masahisa, is said to have felt that Uchimura did not avail himself of important books, and a young missionary was told by more experienced colleagues in the 1920s that Uchimura’s work was plodding and conservative. It is natural that those who prided themselves on their knowledge of contemporary biblical studies would consider Uchimura’s work behind the times. They were right, for Uchimura did not seek to record the degrees to which secular scholarship supported or refuted the claims of the Bible. Instead, he continued an older and more popular tradition that is generally known as “exposition”

of biblical texts: the attempt to glean from a given passage its significance for the life of the contemporary individual. It is a technique common to pulpits throughout the world, and it rests upon an assumption quite different from that of exegesis. This is that the Bible as it exists and without reference to secular sources constitutes a sufficient guide to individuals in their lives. Textual questions do not become a problem to the same extent, and, when research fails, faith takes over. What the Bible says is then “true” in the presentation of its central message that relates humans to God. The truth, where not scientifically and historically demonstrable, remains true in the sense of great myth and allegory. Contradictions between its text and science do not perturb the reader. The fact that the Bible has continued to attract attention for so many generations is seen as sufficient proof of its claim to intimations of the divine. Expositors use their rationality to glean from this ageold repository of wisdom lessons that will serve the concerns of themselves and their audiences. They ask not how the words of the Bible fit into history but how they can serve the present needs of everyone.

Seen in the light of this immediate and practical purpose, the widespread acceptance of Uchimura’s Bible commentary becomes more understandable. By the 1920s, the Bible was widely available in Japanese translation. The large corps of well-trained professionals and businesspeople had learned about the place that the Bible held in the West. Many of them wished to read it, to study English, to understand the West, or to further their own religious quests.

Many of them also felt themselves, like the young Kanzô, caught between competing value systems and willing to hear about this new one. They would buy a Bible only to find it of very little help to them. Uchimura’s Bible study works provided them with a handy guide, organized along the lines of the Bible itself and at every turn linking its words to the concerns of his readers. To one reared in a Sunday school tradition, much of it sounds rudimentary, but many members of the audience had to start from zero. They welcomed such specific information with an enthusiasm that skeptics reared in the Western Christian tradition find hard to understand.

Many Western intellectuals think that their institutions are irrelevant to contemporary needs. The church seems too puny to effect the transformations that the ideals of Jesus demand. And the Bible, easily available in every hotel room and seldom read, has lost its magic. Who understands that a woman might name her infant son Elihu because she admires the courage and conviction of the youthful mediator who interposed himself between the discouraged Job and his detractors? Eighteenth-century Puritan Americans knew. And Uchimura’s works told twentieth-century Japanese.

Finally, Uchimura’s works did not demand that his readers renounce their pasts. Uchimura admired Confucian and Buddhist ideals and saw Christianity as simply an appropriate graft to the stock of the Japanese ethical tradition, while on balance he felt content with the Japanese state. His readers found that this interpretation of tradition suited their own qualified acceptance of the past. Uchimura’s words thus made the Bible relevant to his readers’ needs. This general appeal of his Bible commentary rested upon some very specific elements within it.

The first is his claim that the truth of Bible statements can best be verified by reference to one’s own life experience. Uchimura puts himself and his reader into the position of the biblical character and asks what the character would have felt with assumptions that all people in all ages have reacted basically the same way. In his discussion of Job, Uchimura believed that he had become Job and made his readers feel that they themselves shared in the experience. The introduction of biblical heroes as strong individuals produced a vigorous sense of individual worth and responsibility in readers. In the words of Sekine Masao, there was nothing in Taishô Japan composed of a rising urban middle class and a very conservative agricultural hinterland that could “compare with Uchimura’s biblical exposition for the clarity with which it set forth the true significance of the individual.” In a world dominated by official social ethics, such a view provided an important alternative.

This emphasis on the individual and his or her experience reflected a general intuitive approach to scripture. In the beginning of his lectures on Daniel, for instance, Uchimura pointed out that recent scholarship casts doubts on the historicity of much written in the Bible but that much is also without doubt true to history. This recognition of a conundrum followed by the most intuitive among the possible alternative explanations afforded Uchimura’s love for colourful imagery full leeway. One of his chief deshi, Nambara Shigeru, a distinguished political scientist who later became president of Tokyo University, found Uchimura more of a Christian poet than a scholar.

Finally, those who know other interpretations of the Bible find Uchimura’s work innovative. For instance, though he owned A.B. Davidson’s great interpretation of Job published in 1903, with its eighteen pages devoted to the questions of date and authorship, Uchimura made no reference to these and other problems that absorbed so much of Davidson’s attention.

These characteristics of Uchimura’s Bible studies indicate the precise nature of their appeal that Japanese are likely to label “Japanese” in their attempt to inform foreigners about his influence. His interpretations seemed “Japanese” because they made the Bible come to life for his fellows and because Uchimura did not challenge the major elements of the Japanese tradition but rather saw Christianity as the fulfillment of the highest ideals within that tradition. His readers could accept them as an interpretation of the Bible that accorded with their own experience.

Yet the sweeping generalization inherent in the use of “Japanese” becomes quickly apparent when one tries to define it. The concept seems to go back to the nineteenth century, when Westerners were quick to point out areas in which Japanese artifacts and practices differed from their own. The Japanese could then define these areas in which their local conditions differed from those in the West as the things that set them apart. Over the years, a short list of things that defined Japanese religion became common. It included beautiful Buddhist architectural gems, the Shinto respect for nature, stately gardens. It did not include the nexus of personal relations that governed everyday life. Yet it was these relations that, from a Japanese point of view, set Uchimura’s interpretation of Christianity apart. Young people coming to Uchimura for instruction and lacking the support of church structure fell back upon the roles that society assigned to deshi and their sensei. At first, the study of a foreign religion while in the comfortable embrace of familiar social patterns made it easier to understand new ideas, but as Uchimura began to slow down the power of the Japanese personal relations network reasserted itself. In his final act, as a result, he would disassociate himself from much of his legacy.

The breaking point became Uchimura’s attitude toward the church. Much of the rest of the text will concentrate on this problem after we see how Uchimura moved the place where he delivered his series of lectures from the centre of Tokyo to his suburban home. Although the lectures on the Bible continued up until shortly before his death in 1930, Uchimura had set the pattern for all his later work by these series of lectures that started in the Eiseikai Hall. He lost the use of this highly visible platform when the Great Earthquake of 1 September 1923 levelled it. The event became for Uchimura and the millions who lived through it a major turning point in history, a sensibility completely alien to those who did not share the experience. This analysis of his works in the years when he was most in the public eye ends therefore with a description of how the earthquake affected him.

Uchimura had spent the summer in the mountain resort of Karuizawa, 100 miles to the northwest of Tokyo. He had lived alone in a small rented house as shosei came one at a time from Tokyo to care for his needs. It had been a happy summer, which included relaxed contacts with old friends such as Abe Isô and Ozaki Yukio (1858-1954) (“It has been a great loss for Japan that such a person has not been given the prime minister’s chair.”) On 1 September, the bags were packed for the return to Tokyo when Ishiwara, helping Uchimura, went out to buy bread for lunch. Suddenly, the whole road began to shake like a boat, and walking became difficult. Ishiwara returned home to find Uchimura standing barefoot on the grass, eyes wide with fright. During the night, what looked like “pillars of fire” rose red into the sky in the direction of Tokyo.
